claims.text: The target material is an equimolar bulk HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy.
The target samples are defect-free and contain no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed model separately computes lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The lattice calculation uses DFT-derived interatomic force constants that account for local chemical short-range order.
Local chemical short-range order and lattice distortions modulate phonon scattering and lattice thermal conductivity.
Atomic-scale variations in elemental mass and bonding affect lattice heat transport.
Accounting for short-range order and temperature-dependent dynamics improves predictions of phonon scattering rates.
Increasing temperature can increase phonon scattering and reduce lattice thermal conductivity.
The model will predict lattice thermal conductivity of defect-free HfNbTaTiZr within ±20% of experiment from 300 to 1200 K.
The proposed approach will outperform methods based on Debye-temperature approximations or averaged parameters.
Earlier analytical approaches conflate lattice and electronic heat-transport contributions.
Earlier approaches typically have errors greater than ±20%.
HfNbTaTiZr lattice thermal conductivity will decrease nonlinearly as temperature increases.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity should lie near the reported high-temperature total-conductivity range of 10–17 W/(K m).
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
The model is applicable to oxygen-controlled, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
The model may not apply to samples with significant secondary phases, high impurity levels, or temperatures below 200 K.
Transient thermal grating or phonon-spectroscopy measurements combined with electronic-transport measurements can isolate the lattice contribution.
A deviation exceeding ±20% from the isolated lattice component falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce the predicted nonlinear temperature dependence falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis emphasizes non-conflation and prediction of the lattice component, but the predicted outcome uses the 10–17 W/(K m) total-conductivity range as an example benchmark for lattice conductivity.

Data below 200 K are proposed as validation of the decoupling even though the boundary states that the approach may not hold below 200 K, leaving the status of that validation regime internally unclear.
